hood_landmark.The Strip: Bellagio's dancing fountains amid the mega-casino resorts
hood_landmark.Downtown / Fremont Street: Fremont Street Experience's giant LED canopy over vintage casinos
hood_landmark.Summerlin: Red Rock Canyon's scenic drive on the city's western edge
hood_landmark.Henderson: Lake Las Vegas waterfront resort village
hood_landmark.Chinatown (Spring Mountain): Spring Mountain Road's pan-Asian restaurant plazas anchored by Chinatown Plaza

avoid.reason: Caution off the Strip and downtown/east of Fremont St at night

hood_desc: The Strip is the iconic 4-mile boulevard of mega-resort casinos, shows, clubs and fountains, the classic base for first-time visitors, nightlife and non-stop action.
Downtown and Fremont Street offer vintage neon casinos, a covered light canopy and a cheaper, retro party atmosphere, great for budget travelers and old-school Vegas fans.
Summerlin is an affluent master-planned suburb near Red Rock Canyon with golf, upscale dining and Downtown Summerlin shopping, suited to families and quieter, resort-style stays.
Henderson is a safe, family-friendly suburb southeast of the Strip with parks, lakes and relaxed neighborhoods, appealing to travelers wanting a calm residential base.
Chinatown along Spring Mountain Road is the city's beloved Asian dining district, packed with authentic restaurants and late-night eats, perfect for foodies away from the Strip.

water.note: Tap water is treated and safe to drink, though some prefer bottled for taste.

transit.pay: For RTC buses, buy passes in the rideRTC app or at ticket machines along the Strip: US$6 for 2 hours or US$8 for 24 hours, valid on the Deuce and all buses. The Monorail is separate — singles around US$6 and day passes sold at station kiosks or lvmonorail.com. No transit card needed.
transit.hours: The Deuce runs 24/7 along the Strip; the Monorail runs from 7am until midnight-3am depending on the day.
transit.note: Transit only really covers the Strip and downtown: the Monorail runs behind the east-side casinos and the Deuce runs the Strip itself. Elsewhere, use rideshare or rent a car; free trams link several resorts (e.g. Bellagio-Aria, Mandalay Bay-Excalibur).

food.name: The Vegas buffet
food.desc: Dozens of live stations, crab legs and unlimited everything. Far fewer survive than a decade ago, so the ones left are better curated.

places.name: Bacchanal Buffet
places.note: Nine open kitchens and 250-plus rotating dishes; repeatedly voted the best buffet in Las Vegas.

places.name: The Buffet at Wynn
places.note: Sixteen cooking stations in a bright garden room; the strongest brunch option on the Strip.

places.name: AYCE Buffet
places.note: Best price-to-quality ratio in town, with a strong Asian station and shorter queues.

food.name: Shrimp cocktail
food.desc: The old-Vegas loss leader, introduced downtown in 1959 at 50 cents a glass and still served in a sundae dish with tangy red sauce.

places.name: Saginaw's Delicatessen
places.note: Recreates the original 1959 Golden Gate recipe and sauce after the downtown original disappeared; the real thing.

places.name: Oyster Bar at Palace Station
places.note: Tiny counter beloved by locals; come for the pan roast as well and expect a wait.

food.name: Chinatown noodles and dumplings
food.desc: Spring Mountain Road holds well over 200 Asian restaurants, and locals eat here rather than on the Strip. Hand-pulled noodles, Sichuan heat, dim sum.

places.name: China Mama
places.note: Handmade noodles and soup dumplings at a fraction of Strip prices; the benchmark local Chinese spot.

places.name: Chengdu Taste
places.note: Authentic Sichuan with real numbing heat; toothpick lamb and boiled fish are the orders.

places.name: Sparrow + Wolf
places.note: Asian-inflected Euro-American bistro cooking and one of the best steaks in the city, off the Strip.

food.name: Late-night pizza slice
food.desc: Vegas runs on 3am food. New York-style slices from unmarked hallways and neon-lit rock joints are the classic post-casino move.

places.name: Secret Pizza
places.note: Unmarked record-lined hallway on the third floor, open until 4am; cash-friendly and always packed.

places.name: Evel Pie
places.note: Evel Knievel-themed slice shop open until 4am on weekends, with a jukebox and a serious crust.

places.name: Good Pie
places.note: Detroit and Sicilian squares from a champion pizzaiolo; the quality pick if you are not on the Strip.

food.name: Tijuana-style adobada tacos
food.desc: Trompo-shaved pork and mesquite carne asada on doubled corn tortillas, dressed at a communal salsa bar. The city's true after-midnight staple.

places.name: Tacos El Gordo
places.note: Tijuana import open till 4am on weekends; adobada and suadero are the picks, queue for each meat separately.

places.name: Roberto's Taco Shop
places.note: Open 24 hours across the valley; unglamorous, cheap and exactly what you want at 4am.

food.name: Vegas steakhouse
food.desc: Dry-aged beef, tableside theatre and a wine list the length of an arm. The city has more steakhouses now than at any point in its history.

places.name: Bazaar Meat by Jose Andres
places.note: Reopened in a 20,000 sq ft space in September 2025; Spanish-inflected showmanship and whole-animal cookery.

places.name: Golden Steer Steakhouse
places.note: Rat Pack-era red-leather booths since 1958; order the bone-in ribeye and sit in Sinatra's booth if you can.

places.name: CUT by Wolfgang Puck
places.note: Precise wagyu cookery and famously good service; a reliable big-night-out choice.

food.name: Vintage craft cocktail
food.desc: Vegas has a serious off-Strip bar culture built on pre-Prohibition recipes and original methods, poured late into the night.

places.name: Herbs and Rye
places.note: On North America's 50 Best Bars; a 200-strong list organised by cocktail era, open till 3am.

places.name: Velveteen Rabbit
places.note: Sister-owned, art-filled and playful; the seasonal Creature Feature menu is where the fun is.

food.name: Tiki drinks
food.desc: Rum, fire and fake volcanoes. Vegas leans into tiki maximalism better than almost anywhere, and two of the best bars run around the clock.

places.name: Frankie's Tiki Room
places.note: Open 24 hours, carved tiki interiors and strong, well-made drinks; collect the mug.

places.name: The Golden Tiki
places.note: Shrunken-head hall of fame, animatronics and a proper rum list; a locals' late-night favourite.

landmarks: Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas sign
This retro neon sign at the south end of the Strip is the most photographed roadside marker in Las Vegas and a classic first stop for visitors.
Bellagio Fountains
This choreographed water, music, and light show on the Bellagio's 8.5-acre lake is a free nightly spectacle that draws huge crowds along the Strip.
The Strat (Stratosphere Tower)
At over 1,100 feet, this is the tallest freestanding observation tower in the US, offering panoramic Strip views and thrill rides at its summit.
Eiffel Tower at Paris Las Vegas
A half-scale replica of the Parisian original, this landmark offers an observation deck with sweeping Strip views, especially striking at night.
The Venetian's Grand Canal
Indoor canals with singing gondoliers recreate Venice under a painted sky ceiling, making it one of the Strip's most whimsical photo spots.
Fremont Street Experience
This pedestrian mall in Downtown Vegas is topped by a massive LED canopy that puts on nightly light shows above vintage neon casino signs.
Luxor Las Vegas pyramid
A 30-story black glass pyramid with a giant Sphinx replica out front and the world's most powerful vertical light beam shooting from its apex.
High Roller Observation Wheel
One of the world's tallest observation wheels, its glass cabins offer 360-degree views of the Strip and surrounding desert from 550 feet up.
Caesars Palace
A Roman-themed mega-resort famous for its classical fountains, statues, and colonnades, and a longtime symbol of Las Vegas Strip glamour.
The Sphere
A 366-foot spherical arena wrapped in the world's largest LED screen, opened in 2023 on the Strip for immersive concerts and films.

train.note: Las Vegas has no passenger rail station. Amtrak sells Thruway connecting motorcoaches (book at https://www.amtrak.com/) that link the city to trains at Los Angeles and other California stations, ticketed as part of a single rail journey. The Brightline West high-speed line to Southern California was still under construction in 2026 and is not yet carrying passengers. Until it opens, driving, flying or the coach are the only options.

bus.note: Tufesa's cross-border coaches stop at Mexican immigration - carry your passport (and check US re-entry documents for the return), and pick up an FMM tourist card at the border. Greyhound (https://www.greyhound.com/) and FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/) run frequent domestic services to Los Angeles (about five to six hours), Phoenix (five) and Salt Lake City (eight to nine) from downtown Las Vegas. Most departures are from the Greyhound terminal on South Main Street downtown rather than the Strip, so allow time to get there. Fares are cheapest online in advance.

ferry.note: Las Vegas is in the Mojave Desert and has no ferries. Sightseeing and tour boats operate on nearby Lake Mead, about 45 minutes east, and rafting trips run below Hoover Dam on the Colorado River.

half.name: Grand Canyon West Rim
half.blurb: One of Earth's great natural wonders, with sweeping overlooks and the glass Skywalk bridge.

half.name: Hoover Dam
half.blurb: Colossal Depression-era dam spanning the Colorado River, with tours and bridge views over Black Canyon.

half.name: Red Rock Canyon
half.blurb: Fiery sandstone escarpments and a scenic loop drive offering hiking and climbing right outside town.

half.name: Valley of Fire State Park
half.blurb: Nevada's oldest state park dazzles with flaming red sandstone formations and ancient petroglyphs.

half.name: Death Valley National Park
half.blurb: Stark, otherworldly desert of salt flats, dunes, and the lowest point in North America.

full.name: Zion National Park
full.blurb: Towering red cliffs and the Virgin River carve one of America's most beloved canyon parks.
